title: After Finishing My Study at Tulane University and Freiburg University
paragraphs: From April 2012, I did clerkships for two months at Tulane University in the US, and for three weeks in June at the University of Freiburg in Germany. First, Tulane University is a prestigious university in New Orleans, in the southern United States. New Orleans is a city with a great deal of history, and the influence of the French colonial period remains here and there in the city. The university hospital is in downtown, near the French Quarter, and the city was lively with some event every weekend. I visited the main campus in Uptown during the university festival, and it was quite different: a vast campus in a beautiful residential area next to a large green park, where I could feel the rich atmosphere of the city of New Orleans.
My first month was a clerkship in the ER. Thinking "America means the ER, doesn't it?", I had requested it and studied for it from when my study abroad was first decided, but here I was overwhelmed.

The clerkship consisted of taking the history when a patient came, giving a presentation, and going to see the patient again with the fellow or attending. But on the first day I was just left dumbfounded by how the students worked and by the sheer speed. As the days went by, with truly enthusiastic doctors and kind patients who tried to make out my English, I felt every day that I was becoming able to take histories and give presentations well. Even on the last day I could not think that I was working on a par with the local students, but the experience of getting to know many doctors and students and working with them has become a valuable memory I can never forget.
The second month was hematology. Here, in contrast, I belonged to a small consult team.

The clerkship consisted of seeing patients in the morning and presenting to the fellow, rounds, a conference, and then rounds again with the attending. There were not so many patients, so unlike the quick movement in the ER, it was good to have the opportunity to study one patient slowly. Even so, most of the patients consulted had sickle cell disease as an underlying condition, which is rarely seen in Japan, and this too gave me a series of cases that could only be experienced in a southern American city. At the conferences of the whole hematology department I had many opportunities to talk with foreign doctors working in America, which was a great encouragement to me.

In the gaps in the clerkship, I also went to NY and met classmates who were studying at other universities, which was a refreshing break. At Dr. 兼井's home party I was able to talk with many Japanese doctors, which helped me think about my own career.
The third month was a clerkship in neurosurgery at the University of Freiburg in Germany.

Freiburg is in southwestern Germany, near the French border, and is a quiet university town surrounded by nature. Among the historic buildings there were also many shops, and I thought it was an easy city to live in.
By train I could also easily make one-day trips to nearby France and Switzerland, and even on a day when I overslept until around 11, I could go to Switzerland to play.

Since I cannot speak German, it was impossible to take patients' histories, but it was fulfilling: during the morning rounds I was allowed to do simple procedures, and a neurosurgery resident stayed with me and taught me what I did not understand. There were five operating rooms for neurosurgery alone, with an average of about 12 operations every day, so the abundance of cases was astonishing.

Half of the neurosurgery residents were women, which was very reassuring for me. I remember that when I said that there are almost no women in neurosurgery in Japan, people were surprised and asked why.

Looking back, three months was a short period, but I was able to have such a valuable experience as a medical student, and it became a truly unforgettable experience. The three-month study abroad program of Nagoya University is truly wonderful, and I sincerely thank the professors who created this program and those who have maintained it over the generations. I would also like to take this opportunity to sincerely thank everyone in the International Exchange Office, the professors of Nagoya University, everyone in the Student Affairs Office, the seniors and classmates who gave me advice and mental support, and my family. Thank you very much.
